title: ripgrep
description: ripgrep (rg) — a line-oriented search tool that recursively searches the current directory for a regex pattern, automatically respecting .gitignore rules and skipping hidden files and binaries by default. Written in Rust; generally faster than grep, ag, and ack.

Getting Started.Getting Started:
`ripgrep` is a single self-contained binary called `rg`. No runtime
dependencies, no configuration required to get useful default behavior.

## Install on Arch Linux

```bash
sudo pacman -S ripgrep
```

That's the whole install. `ripgrep` is in the `[extra]` repo and stays
current with upstream releases.

## Install elsewhere

```bash
# macOS
brew install ripgrep

# Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt install ripgrep

# Via cargo (any platform with Rust toolchain)
cargo install ripgrep
```

Prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS, and Windows are also published on every
[GitHub release](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/releases).

## Check your version

```bash
rg --version
```

The current stable line is ripgrep 15.x — 15.0.1 is what most package
managers (including Arch's `extra` repo) are shipping as of late 2026, with
15.1.0 also available as a newer point release. Check the
[releases page](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep/releases) or your
distro's package info for the exact version you have.

## Your first search

```bash
rg "TODO"
```

Run with no path argument, `rg` recursively searches the current directory,
automatically skipping anything ignored by `.gitignore`, hidden files/dirs,
and binary files.

```bash
rg "TODO" lib/          # search a specific directory
rg "TODO" lib/main.dart # search a specific file
```

See [Core Concepts](/ripgrep/core-concepts/) for how the ignore-aware
defaults work and how they differ from plain `grep -r`.
Getting Started.Core Concepts:
## The ignore-aware default

This is ripgrep's headline difference from `grep -r`: by default `rg`
walks the directory tree the same way Git would. It automatically skips:

- Anything matched by `.gitignore` (at any level, plus global gitignore).
- Anything matched by `.ignore` (a ripgrep/The Silver Searcher-specific
  ignore file, useful when you don't want to touch `.gitignore` itself).
- Hidden files and directories (dotfiles), unless you pass `-.`/`--hidden`.
- Binary files, unless you pass `-a`/`--text` or `--binary`.
- The `.git` directory itself.

This means `rg pattern` in a typical project searches only the files a
developer actually cares about — no `node_modules`, no `.dart_tool`, no
build artifacts — with zero configuration.

## Progressively disabling filtering

`rg` uses a `-u` flag that stacks to peel back layers of filtering:

| Flags | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| *(none)* | Full filtering: gitignore + hidden + binary skipped. |
| `-u` | Also search files ignored by `.gitignore`/`.ignore` (same as `--no-ignore`). |
| `-uu` | Also search hidden files/directories (`--no-ignore --hidden`). |
| `-uuu` | Also search binary files (`--no-ignore --hidden --binary`) — "just search everything." |

```bash
rg -uuu "secret_key"   # search absolutely everything, like classic grep -r
```

## Exit status

Same convention as `grep`: `0` if there's a match, `1` if not, `2` on
error. Useful for scripting:

```bash
if rg -q "^TODO" lib/main.dart; then
  echo "still has a top-level TODO"
fi
```

## Regex engine

By default `rg` uses Rust's `regex` crate — effectively an extended regex
(ERE-like) syntax similar to PCRE features minus backreferences and
lookaround, but implemented with guaranteed linear-time matching (no
catastrophic backtracking). For full PCRE features (lookaround,
backreferences), pass `-P`/`--pcre2`, which uses the PCRE2 library instead
and is compiled in on most distro packages, including Arch's.

```bash
rg -P '(?<=user=)\w+' access.log     # lookbehind needs -P
```

See [Pattern Matching & Regex](/ripgrep/pattern-matching-regex/) for the
detail, and [File Filtering](/ripgrep/file-filtering/) for the full set of
flags that control what gets searched.

Guides.Pattern Matching & Regex:
## Default regex syntax

Unescaped by default (no BRE-style backslash requirements like `grep`):

```
.        any character
*  +  ?  quantifiers
()       grouping
|        alternation
{m,n}    bounded repeat
^  $     line anchors
[abc]    character class
\d \w \s  digit / word / whitespace shorthand classes (work by default!)
```

```bash
rg '(foo|bar)\d+'
```

Note the difference from plain `grep`: `\d`, `\w`, `\s`, parentheses, and
`+`/`?` all work without any special flag — ripgrep's default engine is
already ERE/Perl-like in day-to-day syntax, it just doesn't support
backreferences or lookaround without `-P`.

## Case sensitivity

```bash
rg -i "warning"          # force case-insensitive
rg -S "warning"          # smart case: insensitive unless pattern has an uppercase letter
```

`-S`/`--smart-case` is a very commonly aliased default — many people put
`--smart-case` in their `ripgreprc` so `rg Warning` is case-sensitive but
`rg warning` is not.

## Whole word / whole line

```bash
rg -w "cat" file.txt     # word boundary match
rg -x "done" file.txt    # entire line must match
```

## PCRE2 mode (`-P`)

```bash
rg -P '(?<!\$)\bprice\b(?!\d)'   # lookaround
rg -P '(\w+)\s+\1'                # backreference: repeated word
```

## Fixed strings

```bash
rg -F 'a.b[c]' file.txt   # treat pattern as literal, no regex
```

## Multiline matching

Unlike `grep`, ripgrep can match patterns that span multiple lines:

```bash
rg -U 'fn main\(\) \{[\s\S]*?\}'
```

`-U`/`--multiline` changes `^`/`$` to match the start/end of the whole
input by default rather than each line, and lets `.` optionally cross
newlines when combined with `(?s)` or `[\s\S]`.

## Only-matching and replace preview

```bash
rg -o '\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}'          # print only the matched text
rg 'foo' -r 'bar'                    # preview what a find/replace would look like (does NOT edit files)
```

`-r`/`--replace` never modifies files on disk — it only changes what's
printed. To actually edit files in place, pipe through another tool (e.g.
`sd` or `sed`), see [FAQ](/ripgrep/faq/).
Guides.File Filtering:
## Type filters — the flag you'll use constantly

`rg` ships with built-in knowledge of hundreds of file types.

```bash
rg --type-list | head       # see all known types
rg -t dart "TODO"           # search only .dart files
rg -t rust -t toml "version" # search Rust source AND TOML files
rg -T markdown "TODO"        # search everything EXCEPT markdown
```

Define your own on the fly:

```bash
rg --type-add 'web:*.{html,css,js}' -t web "console.log"
```

## Glob filters

For anything not covered by a type, use gitignore-style globs directly:

```bash
rg --glob '*.dart' "TODO"
rg --glob '!*_test.dart' "TODO"       # exclude test files
rg --glob 'lib/**/*.dart' "TODO"      # restrict to a subtree
```

`--glob` (`-g`) can be repeated; each one is ANDed/ORed following gitignore
glob semantics (a leading `!` negates).

## Ignore-file controls

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--no-ignore` | Don't respect `.gitignore`/`.ignore` at all. |
| `--no-ignore-vcs` | Ignore `.gitignore` but still respect `.ignore`. |
| `--no-ignore-parent` | Don't climb parent directories for ignore files. |
| `--hidden` | Also search hidden files/directories. |
| `-.` | Shorthand for `--hidden`. |
| `--binary` | Also search binary files. |

```bash
rg --hidden --glob '!.git' "api_key"
```

This is the idiomatic way to search dotfiles (like `.env`) while still
explicitly excluding `.git`.

## Depth and symlinks

```bash
rg --max-depth 2 "TODO"
rg --follow "TODO"        # follow symlinks (off by default)
```

See [Common Options](/ripgrep/common-options/) for output-formatting flags
and [Recipes](/ripgrep/recipes/) for these combined into real workflows.
Guides.Common Options:
## Output control

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-n` / `--line-number` | Show line numbers (on by default in terminal, off when piped). |
| `-N` | Never show line numbers. |
| `-c` | Count matching lines per file. |
| `--count-matches` | Count total match occurrences, not just matching lines. |
| `-l` | Only print filenames with a match. |
| `--files-without-match` | Only print filenames with no match. |
| `-o` | Print only the matched text. |
| `-A/-B/-C NUM` | After/before/both context lines. |
| `--json` | Emit structured JSON per match (great for tooling/editor integration). |
| `-p` / `--pretty` | Force color and headings even when piped (implies `--heading --color=always`). |

```bash
rg -C 3 "panic" app.log
rg --json "error" | jq .
```

## Listing files

```bash
rg --files                  # list every file rg would search (respects ignore rules)
rg --files -t dart           # list only .dart files it would search
rg --files | rg 'config'     # find files by name (not content)
```

This is the ripgrep-native replacement for `find . -name` in a
gitignore-aware project.

## Sorting

```bash
rg --sort path "TODO"        # deterministic output order
rg --sort modified "TODO"    # most-recently-modified logic depends on direction flag
```

By default `rg`'s output order is not guaranteed (it searches in parallel
across threads for speed) — use `--sort` when order matters, e.g. in CI
logs or diffs.

## Context and grouping in terminal output

```bash
rg --heading "TODO"      # group matches under a filename heading (default when using a terminal)
rg --no-heading "TODO"   # prefix every line with filename:line instead (default when piped)
```

## Performance-related flags

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `-j NUM` / `--threads NUM` | Cap worker threads (rg auto-detects cores by default). |
| `--mmap` | Force memory-mapped I/O (can help on some large single files). |
| `-z` / `--search-zip` | Search inside gzip/bzip/xz/zstd-compressed files. |

See [Recipes](/ripgrep/recipes/) for these assembled into full workflows.
Guides.Recipes:
## Search only source files, ignoring build output

```bash
rg -t dart "print(" lib/
```

No `--exclude-dir=build` needed — `.gitignore` already covers it in a
typical Dart project.

## Find every file matching a name pattern (not content)

```bash
rg --files -g '*.g.dart'
```

## Search including dotfiles but not .git

```bash
rg --hidden -g '!.git' "API_KEY"
```

## Grep JSON logs for a field, structured output

```bash
rg --json '"level":"error"' app.log | jq -r '.data.lines.text'
```

## Case-insensitive search across the whole repo, ignoring tests

```bash
rg -i -g '!*_test.dart' "deprecated"
```

## Preview a rename before actually doing it

```bash
rg 'oldFunctionName' -r 'newFunctionName'
```

This only shows what *would* change. To actually apply it across files,
pipe filenames into `sd` (a modern `sed` replacement, also Rust-based) or
use `sed -i` per match:

```bash
rg -l 'oldFunctionName' | xargs sd 'oldFunctionName' 'newFunctionName'
```

## Search compressed logs directly

```bash
rg -z "OutOfMemoryError" /var/log/app/*.log.gz
```

## Use as a fast `find`-by-content in scripts

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
if rg -q --type dart "class .*extends StatelessWidget" lib/; then
  echo "widgets present"
fi
```

## Persist personal defaults with an rgrc file

```bash
# ~/.config/ripgrep/config (any path, referenced via RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH)
--smart-case
--hidden
--glob=!.git/
```

```bash
export RIPGREP_CONFIG_PATH="$HOME/.config/ripgrep/config"
```

Put this export in your shell profile (`~/.bashrc`, `~/.zshrc`) so every
`rg` invocation picks up your preferred defaults.

Project.FAQ:
### How is this different from plain `grep -r`?

`ripgrep` respects `.gitignore` automatically, skips hidden files and
binaries by default, and searches in parallel across CPU cores — so it's
both more convenient in a typical project and substantially faster on
large trees. `grep -r` does neither of those by default. See
[Core Concepts](/ripgrep/core-concepts/).

### Does ripgrep edit files in place?

No. `-r`/`--replace` only changes what's *printed*; it never writes to
disk. Combine `rg -l` with `sd` or `sed -i` to actually apply changes — see
[Recipes](/ripgrep/recipes/).

### Why isn't ripgrep finding a match I know is there?

Almost always one of the default filters. Try progressively:

```bash
rg -u "pattern"     # bypass .gitignore
rg -uu "pattern"    # also search hidden files
rg -uuu "pattern"   # also search binary files, ignore everything
```

If `-uuu` finds it, something in your ignore rules or hidden-file
filtering was excluding the file.

### Do I need `-P` for `\d` and `\w`?

No — those work in ripgrep's default Rust-regex engine already. You only
need `-P`/`--pcre2` for backreferences (`\1`) or lookaround
(`(?=...)`, `(?<=...)`), which the default engine deliberately doesn't
support (it guarantees linear-time matching, which backreferences and
lookaround can't).

### Is ripgrep available on Arch Linux by default?

Not preinstalled, but it's a single `pacman -S ripgrep` away and stays in
sync with upstream releases through the `extra` repository.

### Where do I report bugs or see the changelog?

The project lives at
[github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep](https://github.com/BurntSushi/ripgrep),
maintained by Andrew Gallant (BurntSushi). Releases and changelogs are
published there, and a browsable changelog is also mirrored at
[ripgrep.dev/changelog](https://ripgrep.dev/changelog/).
